Description.Abstract: Null encryption keys can compromise security in a way that is not easy to remedy.
Description.Recommendations: Encryption keys should never be null and should generally be obfuscated and managed in an external source. Storing encryption keys, null or otherwise, in plain text anywhere on the system allows anyone with sufficient permissions to read and potentially misuse the encryption key. Starting with Microsoft(R) Windows(R) 2000, Microsoft(R) provides Windows Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI), which is an OS-level service that protects sensitive application data, such as passwords and encryption keys [1].

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Key Management: Null Encryption Key

Tips.Tip: When identifying null, empty, or hardcoded encryption keys, default rules only consider fields and variables that contain the words enc_key, encryption_key, passphrase, or pass_phrase. However, the Fortify Custom Rules Editor provides the Password Management wizard that makes it easy to create rules for detecting key management issues on custom-named fields and variables.

Due to the dynamic nature of PHP, you may see a large number of findings in PHP library files. Consider using a filter file to hide specific findings from view. For instructions on creating a filter file, see the Fortify Static Code Analyzer User Guide.

Description.Abstract: An empty salt contradicts its intended objective and can compromise system security in a way that is not easy to remedy.
Description.Explanation:
It is never a good idea to use an empty salt. Not only does an empty salt defeat its own purpose but all of the project's developers can view the salt. It makes fixing the problem extremely difficult because after the code is in production, the salt cannot be easily changed. If attackers know the value of the salt, they can compute "rainbow tables" for the application and easily determine the hashed values. In this case, an empty salt was found in the call to in on line . Example 1: The following code defines an empty salt for password hashing: 
...
define('SECURE_AUTH_SALT', "");
...
This code runs successfully, but anyone who has access to it can see the salt. After the program ships, there is likely no way to change the empty salt. An employee with access to this information can use it to break into the system.
Description.Recommendations:
The salt should never be an empty string and should generally be obfuscated and managed in an external source. Storing a salt in plain text anywhere on the system allows anyone with sufficient permissions to read and potentially misuse the salt. Example 2: The following code defines a salt variable configured by the system administrator: 
...
define('SECURE_AUTH_SALT', $salt);
...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Weak Cryptographic Hash: Empty Salt

Description.Abstract: A hardcoded salt can compromise system security in a way that is not easy to remedy.
Description.Explanation:
It is never a good idea to hardcode a salt. Not only does a hardcoded salt allow all of the project's developers to view the salt, it also makes fixing the problem extremely difficult. After the code is in production, the salt cannot be easily changed. If attackers know the value of the salt, they can compute "rainbow tables" for the application and more easily determine the hashed values. In this case, a hardcoded salt was found in the call to in on line . Example 1: The following code uses a hardcoded salt: 
    ...
    crypt($password, '2!@$(5#@532@%#$253l5#@$');
    ...
This code will run successfully, but anyone who has access to it will have access to the salt. After the program ships, there is likely no way to change the salt "2!@$(5#@532@%#$253l5#@$". An employee with access to this information can use it to break into the system.
Description.Recommendations:
The salt should never be hardcoded and should generally be obfuscated and managed in an external source. Storing a salt in plain text anywhere on the system allows anyone with sufficient permissions to read and potentially misuse the salt. Example 2: The following code uses a salt variable configured by the system administrator: 
    ...
    crypt($password, $salt);
    ...

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Weak Cryptographic Hash: Hardcoded Salt
